Laboratory stocks of Cyclops vicinus reared at a constant water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] provided detailed morphometric data across the life cycle. Newly hatched nauplii, emerging from subitaneous eggs following a brief incubation period, measured just 0.0207 cm [Lb = 0.0207 cm] in total body length, a diminutive size that underscores the substantial proportional growth this species must achieve. This initial length at birth serves as a critical baseline for quantifying the rapid somatic expansion that occurs during the subsequent copepodite stages. The transition from the yolk-dependent nauplius to the first feeding copepodite marks the onset of exogenous feeding, a trophic switch that fuels accelerated growth. Observations of cohort development under standardized laboratory conditions allowed precise determination of these early size benchmarks, which are essential for constructing accurate growth trajectories. The pronounced difference between the neonatal length and the dimensions attained by later instars highlights the considerable developmental demands placed upon juvenile copepods as they navigate a pelagic environment where size itself governs predation risk and foraging efficiency. Such baseline data are increasingly valuable for comparative studies examining how thermal regimes shape the early life histories of freshwater cyclopoids.

Following the onset of active feeding and the transition through successive copepodite instars, individuals undergo a distinctive metamorphic event that marks the boundary between the juvenile and pre-adult phases. At this critical developmental juncture, the total body length of Cyclops vicinus reaches approximately 0.0626 cm , a measurement recorded at the moment of metamorphosis from the final copepodite stage. This metamorphic length represents a key inflection point in the species' ontogenetic trajectory, reflecting the cumulative growth achieved during the accelerating juvenile period when food intake and assimilation rates are at their peak relative to body size. The value of 0.0626 cm  at metamorphosis provides a quantifiable marker for the completion of larval somatic development and the onset of the morphological reorganization that precedes reproductive maturation. Field ecologists have noted that attaining this size before the onset of seasonal temperature declines may confer a survival advantage, as larger copepodites are better equipped to withstand winter conditions and emerge earlier in the following spring. The precision of this measurement, derived from repeated microscopic examination of exuviae, allows for robust comparisons across populations inhabiting different thermal environments.

Sexual maturation in Cyclops vicinus culminates in the attainment of puberty, a stage characterized by the onset of gametogenesis and the development of secondary sexual characteristics visible in the antennules and urosome morphology. At this pubertal transition, individuals have achieved a total body length of 0.1627 cm [Lp = 0.1627 cm], a size that also represents the ultimate total length (0.1627 cm) [Li = 0.1627 cm] reached by this species, as growth effectively ceases upon reproductive activation. The convergence of the pubertal length and the ultimate total length at 0.1627 cm [Li = 0.1627 cm] [Lp = at 0.1627 cm] indicates that Cyclops vicinus follows a determinate growth pattern in which somatic expansion is largely finalized by the time the first clutch of eggs is produced. This life-history strategy contrasts with that of some other cyclopoid congeners that continue to increase in size incrementally throughout their adult lives. The relatively modest ultimate body size of this species, with adults rarely exceeding two millimeters in length, reflects a trade-off between rapid generation time and the energetic demands of producing large, yolky eggs. Once females reach this terminal size, their energetic budget shifts almost entirely toward reproductive investment, a transition confirmed by the absence of further molting events.

Reproductive output in female Cyclops vicinus maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] is characterized by a combination of moderate clutch size and relatively short interclutch intervals. Females typically produce a single clutch of 110 eggs [N_R_i = single clutch of 110 eggs] during each reproductive episode, a fecundity value that aligns with the mid-range observed among temperate cyclopoids of comparable body size. The interval between successive clutches is approximately three days, yielding a frequency of one clutch every three days [F_R_i = one clutch every three days] under optimal feeding conditions on a mixed diet of algae and rotifers. This rapid turnover allows a single ovigerous female to generate multiple broods across her reproductive lifespan, contributing substantially to population growth during favorable thermal windows. The consistency of the 110 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 110 eggs per clutch] and the three-day clutch interval [F_R_i = the three-day clutch interval] underscores the reliance of this species on a mixed diet to meet the elevated energetic demands of continuous egg production. These reproductive parameters, measured in the laboratory, provide a mechanistic basis for understanding how Cyclops vicinus achieves numerical dominance in eutrophic lakes during the spring phytoplankton bloom.

Longevity records for Cyclops vicinus indicate that adult females maintained at a constant temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] have a maximum lifespan of 44 days [am = 44 days], a relatively abbreviated adult duration characteristic of small-bodied cyclopoids with high metabolic rates and continuous reproductive activity. The coupling of a short adult lifespan with a rapid reproductive rate — including clutches of 110 eggs repeated every three days — allows this species to achieve high intrinsic population growth despite individual brief longevity. In natural habitats, temperature fluctuations can extend or contract this lifespan; individuals experiencing cooler spring conditions may persist somewhat longer than the 44 days [am = 44 days] recorded in the laboratory, though at the cost of reduced clutch frequency at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. The physiological death of post-reproductive females typically occurs after the cessation of egg production, marking the completion of the organismal lifespan. These demographic constraints collectively define the ecological role of Cyclops vicinus as a rapidly cycling herbivore and microcarnivore in temperate freshwater plankton communities.
